query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Implement an integrated in-situ experimental approach combining high-speed synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD) with rapid scanning calorimetry to directly observe melting and quantify fusion thermodynamic properties of HEAs in real time.
generation.material_initial_state: Polycrystalline HEA samples with homogeneous microstructures, minimal impurities, and uniform grain size distributions.
generation.intervention: Simultaneously perform high-speed synchrotron XRD and rapid scanning calorimetry in a controlled, inert atmosphere furnace to monitor dynamic structural changes and corresponding heat flow during the melting transition.
generation.conditions: Experiments must be carried out under an inert atmosphere with high temporal resolution (sub-second) and precise synchronization between XRD detectors and calorimetric sensors; suitable for HEAs with moderate melting points and stable liquid phases.
generation.structural_mediator: Real-time XRD captures lattice parameter evolution, phase coexistence, and volume changes, while concurrent calorimetry directly measures heat flow; the correlation between these signals mediates extraction of thermodynamic parameters.
generation.mechanism: The technique directly correlates the onset of structural disordering (transition from crystalline to liquid-like diffraction patterns) with the endothermic peak in calorimetry, enabling quantitative determination of melting temperature, enthalpy, entropy, and volume change with minimal model dependence.
generation.predicted_outcome: Fusion property measurements (Tm, ∆H_fusion, ∆S_fusion, and volume change) will be obtained with high temporal resolution and quantitative accuracy within a 5% error margin relative to standard DSC and dilatometry data.
generation.baseline: Traditional ex-situ DSC or high-temperature XRD individually do not provide the dynamic coupling between structure and thermodynamics; their decoupled measurements leave transient phenomena unobserved.
generation.boundary: Limited by synchrotron flux, detector speed, and sample environment constraints; best applied to HEAs that do not degrade or react under high-temperature X-ray exposure.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties may arise from synchronization issues, potential beam-induced effects, and limits in detector resolution; these are mitigated by rigorous calibration protocols and optimized beam conditions. We maintain that these uncertainties are minor compared to the benefits of coupled in-situ measurements.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform an integrated in-situ experiment on a well-characterized HEA sample. Validate by confirming that the structural disorder detected by XRD synchronizes with the calorimetric endotherm, and compare the derived fusion properties with those obtained from standard DSC and dilatometry.
measurements: Time-resolved XRD patterns showing phase fraction evolution
Simultaneously recorded calorimetric heat flow curves
Correlation between structural transitions and calorimetric peaks
Quantitative fusion enthalpy and melting temperature extraction
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the temporal alignment between XRD changes and calorimetric signals is inconsistent or if the derived fusion properties differ by more than 10% from benchmark measurements, the integrated in-situ approach is deemed invalid.

cited_evidence.text: The maximum volume phase fraction of the sigma phase of 0.1854 was at 430 °C, and as reported, the sigma phase is usually distributed along the grain boundaries []. Formation of the sigma phase was reported by Otto et al., when CrMnFeCoNi HEA was aged for 500 days at 700 °C, while BBC formed at 500 °C, and only FCC was reported to form at 900 °C when held for the same ageing time []. In the microstructure of as-cast alloys, there exist inhomogeneities caused by the partitioning of high melting point/slow diffusing elements from fast diffusing/low melting point elements []. These inhomogeneities give rise to variations not only in composition but also in the solidus temperature, which represents the temperature at which incipient melting occurs. In Figure 9, an inset of the equilibrium composition of the sigma phase is observed, which has a high concentration of Cr followed by Fe and Mn, also confirmed by experimental work []. Some other studies on the long-term stability of the alloy report results as summarised in Table 3. CALPHAD predictions provide information on the phase equilibria at the heat treatment temperature, as well as the solvus and equilibrium solidus temperatures. A

AbstractA systematic study on a face‐centered cubic‐based compositionally complex alloy system Al–Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni in its single‐phase state is carried out, where a mother senary compound Al8Co17Cr17Cu8Fe17Ni33 and five of its suballoys, obtained by removing one element at a time, are investigated and exhaustively analyzed determining the contribution of each alloying element in the solid solution. The senary and the quinaries are compared using experimental techniques including X‐ray absorption spectroscopy, X‐ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and first principles hybrid Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics simulations. Chemical short‐range order and bond length distances have been determined both at the experimental and computational level. Electronic structure and local atomic distortions up to 5.2 Å have been correlated to the microhardness values.
